title: Virus Talk with Josh and Chuck
summary: Josh and Chuck, with Josh sick with a sinus infection, explain what viruses are and how they work. They cover whether viruses are alive, their size and structure (virion, capsid, envelope, DNA or RNA), how they hijack host cells, retroviruses and latency, how colds and flu spread and how long people are contagious, fever as an immune defense, HIV and herpes, and prevention tips such as handwashing and not sharing bodily fluids. They note antibiotics do not treat viral infections, and that mucus color does not reveal the type of infection. The episode closes with a listener email about churchyard burials during the plague and the Black Death, which was bacterial.

segments.title: Opening banter and Josh's illness
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about Josh's stuffy nose and sickness, and mention past episodes on Ebola and HIV. They introduce viruses as operating between living and nonliving.

segments.title: Are viruses alive?
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the debate over whether viruses are living. They explain that cells are the smallest living units and that viruses cannot sustain or reproduce themselves on their own. They also cover theories of origin, including that viruses may be former cell fragments.

segments.title: Virus size, structure and virion
segments.summary: Viruses are about a millionth of an inch long and smaller than bacteria. A virion is an individual viral particle made of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) inside a protein capsid, sometimes with a lipid envelope. Shapes include helical, polyhedral and complex.

segments.title: How viruses enter and hijack cells
segments.summary: Viruses attach to host cells using matching proteins and either inject genetic material or enter as a whole particle. Inside, they take over the cell's enzymes and machinery to make more viruses, described as a hostile takeover.

segments.title: Retroviruses and how new viruses leave the cell
segments.summary: Retroviruses insert their genetic material into the host cell's DNA and can stay quiet. Naked viruses burst out and destroy the cell, while enveloped viruses bud off with the cell membrane. HIV and flu are mentioned as retroviruses, and the hosts note the retrovirus mention of flu is uncertain.

segments.title: Josh's cold, sinus infection and how colds spread
segments.summary: Josh describes his symptoms and the hosts discuss how a virus is inhaled or enters through broken skin, attacks nasal and throat cells, and causes runny nose, sore throat and aches. Cell damage and inflammation are described as the cause of symptoms.

segments.title: When you are contagious
segments.summary: People are contagious about a day before symptoms appear. Colds are contagious from a day before symptoms to about four days after, and flu from a day before to five to seven days after. People often think they are no longer contagious too early.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A break in the episode, with no sponsor content described in the transcript.

segments.title: Fever as immune defense
segments.summary: The hosts explain that fever slows body processes, including viral spread, and that some viruses such as Ebola and HIV attack immune cells. Normal body temperature is discussed, and the 98.6 figure is said to be an average that has been questioned.

segments.title: Latency, herpes and HIV sleeping viruses
segments.summary: Some viruses, including HIV and herpes simplex, can lie dormant for years and flare up with triggers such as stress or UV light. Latent viral DNA can be copied as the host cell divides, so many cells can later produce viruses at once.

segments.title: How viruses spread and prevention
segments.summary: Viruses spread by carrier organisms such as mosquitoes and fleas, through the air, through bodily fluids, and via contaminated surfaces where flu virus can survive for days. The hosts recommend frequent handwashing, explaining soap binds germs so rinsing removes them, and covering coughs and sneezes.

segments.title: Antibiotics, virus age and vaccines
segments.summary: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections. Older viruses tend to cause less harm, and humans carry fossilized viral DNA from ancient retroviruses. Vaccines pre-expose the body to a virus, and viruses change enough that vaccines must be updated.

segments.title: Mucus color myth
segments.summary: The hosts address the belief that mucus color reveals whether an infection is viral or bacterial, and say that is not true.

segments.title: Listener mail: Headstones
segments.summary: Listener George Gilbert writes that churchyard burials began because churches sold burial spots inside and near walls, and that burials moved outside during the plague. The hosts note the plague was bacterial, not viral.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts explain how to send listener mail and point listeners to the show's website.
